title: Erdős Problem #889: New Prime Factors in Consecutive Integers
description: Let $v(n,k)$ count prime factors of $n+k$ not dividing $n+i$ for $i < k$. Does $v_0(n) = \max_k v(n,k) \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$? Known: $v_0(n) \ge 2$ for $n \ge 17$. OPEN.

originalContributions: Defined newPrimeFactorCount v(n,k) via Finset.filter on primeFactors with universal non-divisibility check
Defined v₀(n) as iSup of v(n,k) over Finset.range, capturing the extremal new prime count
Formalized the main conjecture ErdosProblem889 as divergence in ε-N form
Axiomatized the complete exception list (v0_exceptions: v₀(n) ≤ 1 ↔ n ∈ {0,1,2,3,4,7,8,16}); the Erdős–Selfridge bound v₀(n) ≥ 2 for n ≥ 17 is derived as a theorem (v0_ge_2_for_large), not an axiom
Defined the generalized vShifted (v_l) and the exact power variant exactPowerNewCount (V(n,k))
Established the comparison V(n,k) ≥ v(n,k) relating the exact power variant to the base version

overview.historicalContext: Erdős and Selfridge introduced $v(n,k)$ in their 1967 paper 'Some problems on the prime factors of consecutive integers' (Illinois J. Math. 11, pp. 428–430). They proved $v_0(n) \ge 2$ for all $n \ge 17$ by analyzing how prime factors distribute across consecutive integers, and determined the complete exception list $\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 16\}$ by explicit computation. However, they could not establish divergence of $v_0(n)$, nor even prove $v_1(n) \ge 2$ for all large $n$. The problem also appears as B27 in Guy's 'Unsolved Problems in Number Theory' (3rd ed., 2004). The question is connected to the broader study of how prime factors distribute across arithmetic progressions and consecutive integers, touching on the Erdős–Kac theorem, Selberg's sieve, and the distribution of smooth numbers.
overview.problemStatement: Let $v(n,k)$ count the prime factors of $n+k$ that do not divide $n+i$ for $0 \le i < k$. Let $v_0(n) = \max_{k \ge 0} v(n,k)$. **Does $v_0(n) \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$?**
overview.text: Let $v(n,k)$ count prime factors of $n+k$ not dividing $n+i$ for $i < k$. Does $v_0(n) = \max_k v(n,k) \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$? Known: $v_0(n) \ge 2$ for $n \ge 17$. OPEN.
overview.proofStrategy: The formalization defines `newPrimeFactorCount` via `Finset.filter` on `primeFactors`, checking non-divisibility at all earlier positions. The extremal function `v₀` uses `iSup` over `Finset.range`. The main conjecture is stated as a `def` (proposition definition), while only the complete exception list is axiomatized (`v0_exceptions`); the Erdős–Selfridge bound $v_0(n) \ge 2$ for $n \ge 17$ is then derived as a theorem (`v0_ge_2_for_large`) from `v0_exceptions` by `omega`. The file also formalizes the generalized version $v_l$ (restricting shifts to $k \ge l$), the exact power variant $V(n,k)$ (using $p$-adic valuation instead of bare divisibility), and the comparison $V \ge v$.
keyInsights: $v(n,k)$ captures genuinely new prime factors at position $k$: primes that divide $n+k$ but none of $n, n+1, \ldots, n+k-1$, measuring the 'novelty' of each term's factorization
Erdős–Selfridge (1967) proved $v_0(n) \ge 2$ for $n \ge 17$ with exactly 8 exceptions, but the gap between this constant lower bound and the conjectured divergence remains completely open
The generalized version $v_l(n) = \max_{k \ge l} v(n,k)$ asks whether divergence persists even when small shifts are excluded, testing whether the phenomenon is robust or an artifact of initial terms
The exact power variant $V(n,k)$ uses $p$-adic valuation ($p^{v_p(n+k)} \nmid n+i$) instead of bare divisibility ($p \nmid n+i$), giving $V \ge v$ and potentially being more tractable
The problem connects to the distribution of smooth numbers: if $n+k$ has many large prime factors, most will be 'new' since large primes are unlikely to divide nearby integers

sections.title: New Prime Factor Count $v(n,k)$
sections.summary: Defines `newPrimeFactorCount n k` as the cardinality of prime factors of $n+k$ that do not divide any $n+i$ for $0 \le i < k$, using `Finset.filter` on `primeFactors` with universal non-divisibility. Includes `newPrimeFactorCount_zero` lemma.
sections.mathContext: Formal definition: Defines `newPrimeFactorCount n k` as the cardinality of prime factors of $n+k$ that do not divide any $n+i$ for $0 \le i < k$, using `Finset.filter` on `primeFactors` with universal non-divisibility.

sections.title: The Maximum $v_0(n)$
sections.summary: Defines `v₀ n` as $\sup_{0 \le k \le n} v(n,k)$ using `iSup` over `Finset.range (n+1)`, the maximum new prime factor count over all shifts.
sections.mathContext: Formal definition: Defines `v₀ n` as $\sup_{0 \le k \le n} v(n,k)$ using `iSup` over `Finset.range (n+1)`, the maximum new prime factor count over all shifts.

sections.title: The Conjecture: $v_0(n) \to \infty$
sections.summary: States `ErdosProblem889` as a `Prop`: $\forall M,\, \exists N_0,\, \forall n \ge N_0,\, v_0(n) > M$. Defined rather than axiomatized since the problem is open.
sections.mathContext: Defined as a `Prop`, not axiomatized: `ErdosProblem889` states $\forall M,\, \exists N_0,\, \forall n \ge N_0,\, v_0(n) > M$. The conjecture itself is left unproved (no axiom asserts it).

sections.title: Known Results: $v_0(n) \ge 2$
sections.summary: Axiomatizes the complete exception list as a biconditional `v0_exceptions: v₀ n ≤ 1 ↔ n ∈ {0,1,2,3,4,7,8,16}`. The Erdős–Selfridge (1967) bound `v0_ge_2_for_large` ($v_0(n) \ge 2$ for $n \ge 17$) is then derived as a theorem.
sections.mathContext: One axiom (`v0_exceptions`) plus one derived theorem (`v0_ge_2_for_large`). The exception biconditional is the only assumption; the bound for $n \ge 17$ follows by `omega` on the complement.

sections.title: Generalized Version $v_l$
sections.summary: Defines `vShifted l n` ($v_l$) restricting shifts to $k \ge l$, states `ErdosProblem889General` (divergence for all $l$), and proves `general_implies_base` as a theorem (specialize `l = 0`).
sections.mathContext: Formal definitions plus one proved theorem: `general_implies_base : ErdosProblem889General → ErdosProblem889` is `fun hGen M => hGen 0 M`, not an axiom.

sections.title: Finiteness of $v_1(n) = 1$
sections.summary: Section header and a docstring posing the weaker subproblem `Does v₁(n) = 1 have only finitely many solutions?`. No declarations are introduced — only commentary noting that even this was beyond Erdős–Selfridge's methods.
sections.mathContext: Informal docstring commentary only. No `axiom`, `theorem`, or `def` is declared in this section; the corresponding shifted variant `vShifted 1` is defined in Section V.

sections.title: Exact Power Variant $V(n,k)$
sections.summary: Defines `exactPowerNewCount` ($V(n,k)$) using $p$-adic valuation, `exactPowerShifted` ($V_l$), and proves the comparison theorem `exact_power_ge_new_prime`: $V(n,k) \ge v(n,k)$. The $V_1$ finiteness question appears only as docstring commentary.
sections.mathContext: Formal definitions plus one proved theorem: `exact_power_ge_new_prime` shows $V(n,k) \ge v(n,k)$ via `Finset.card_le_card` and the fact that `p ^ α ∣ m → p ∣ m` for `α ≠ 0`.

conclusion.summary: Erdős Problem #889 asks whether the maximum count of new prime factors in consecutive integers diverges. Erdős and Selfridge (1967) proved $v_0(n) \ge 2$ for $n \ge 17$ with 8 explicit exceptions, but divergence remains open after nearly 60 years. The formalization captures the core definitions, the known lower bound, the generalized $v_l$ conjecture, and the exact power variant $V(n,k)$ with 0 sorries.
conclusion.implications: Resolution would reveal fundamental growth properties of prime factor distributions in consecutive integer sequences. A proof of divergence would show that arbitrarily long runs of consecutive integers must eventually contain terms with many 'genuinely new' prime factors, connecting to sieve theory and the distribution of smooth numbers.
openQuestions: Does $v_0(n) \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$? Even a bound $v_0(n) \ge 3$ for large $n$ would be new
Does $v_l(n) \to \infty$ for every fixed $l$? This generalization tests robustness against excluding small shifts
Does $v_1(n) = 1$ have only finitely many solutions? This weaker subproblem was already beyond Erdős–Selfridge's methods
Is the exact power variant $V_1(n) > 1$ for all large $n$ more tractable, as Erdős and Selfridge suggested?

crossReferences.description: The prime number theorem governs the asymptotic density of primes, which determines how many 'new' prime factors are available at each position in consecutive integer sequences
Erdős #795 (distinct subset products) also studies the multiplicative structure of integers through prime factorization, sharing the theme of how primes distribute across structured sets
Erdős #892 (primitive sequence domination) studies antichains in the divisibility order, directly relevant to understanding divisibility constraints between consecutive integers
